subject: history_social
passage: In kabaddi, a team sport played across South Asia, a "raider" crosses into the opposing half of the court, tries to touch as many defenders as possible, and must return to his own half without taking a breath. Under the traditional rules, the raider must also chant the word "kabaddi" aloud without pause for the whole of the raid; a raider whose chant stops is ruled out. Sports historian Arjun Bhattacharya notes that an official standing at the edge of the court cannot see whether a player has inhaled, and that a person cannot keep chanting steadily while breathing in. Considered in this light, the chanting rule most likely exists to ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: frighten the defenders by allowing the raider to make as much noise as possible.
choices.B: make the no-breath rule enforceable by turning an invisible act into an audible one.
choices.C: replace the no-breath rule, which officials had found impossible to enforce.
choices.D: give raiders a way to hold their breath for longer than they otherwise could.

explanation.why: The breath rule has a problem: an official cannot see whether a raider has inhaled. The text supplies the missing link, that steady chanting is impossible while breathing in. A raider who keeps chanting has therefore not inhaled, and a chant that stops gives the official something to hear. The chant lets the breath rule be enforced.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never connects the chant to intimidation; it connects it to breathing and to what officials can detect.
explanation.B: Correct. Officials cannot see a breath, but they can hear a chant stop, and chanting cannot continue through an inhalation, so the chant is the breath rule made audible.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The chant supports the breath rule rather than replacing it; both rules apply to the raider.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Chanting uses up air; the text presents it as a check on breathing, not as a way to extend a breath.
